headline: Approved allowing cannabis retailers in the I-40 zone by Special Permit, and a new Mixed Use floating zone
summary: Most speakers opposed the cannabis retailer change, and the applicant cited a 3% municipal tax and 11 jobs. The Mixed Use zone requires at least 40 acres, at least 35% residential space, and a 50-foot height cap. Two projects were continued to December, and the Center Street Cemetery discussion was tabled.
decisions: Continued the Atlantis Management Group gas station special permit at 124 Church St. to the December meeting.
Continued the Times Microwave Systems site plan at 358 Hall Avenue to the December meeting.
Approved the minutes of the October 14, 2026 meeting as submitted, 5-0.
Approved text amendment allowing cannabis retailers by Special Permit in the I-40 zone, 3-2.
Approved Mixed Use floating zone text amendment with changes, 4-1.
Tabled the discussion on violations at Center Street Cemetery until the December meeting.
Noted eight administrative approvals as approved.

plain_text:
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 1 
 
Wallingford Planning & Zoning Commission 
Regular Meeting 
Monday, November 9, 2026 
7:00 p.m. 
Robert F. Parisi Council Chambers – Town Hall 
Town Hall – 45 South Main Street 
MINUTES 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons called the meeting to order at approximately 7:00 p.m.  
 
The Pledge of Allegiance was recited by all. 
Roll Call:  Present:  James Fitzsimmons, Chair; Jeffrey Kohan, Vice Chair; David Leonardo, Secretary; 
James Seichter, Regular Member; J.P. Venoit, Regular Member; Joseph Sanders, Alternate; Richard 
Benham, Alternate; Casey Camire, Alternate; and Kevin Pagini, Town Planner. 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons noted that the following agenda items will not be heard tonight.  
3. PUBLIC HEARING – Special Permit request for Atlantis Management Group to demolish an 
existing building and construct a gas station with a 4,500± sq. ft. drive-through retail and 
convenience store at 124 Church St., located in the I-40 (Industrial) District #407-26. 
Continued to December meeting. 
4. SITE PLAN APPROVAL - Site Plan/Times Microwave Systems/358 Hall Avenue #224-26  
Continued to December meeting. 
 
Consideration of Minutes – October 14, 2026, Regular Meeting 
Commissioner Kohan:  Motion to approve the Minutes of Monday, October 14, 2026, 2026, 
Meeting of the Wallingford Planning and Zoning Commission as submitted. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo:  Second 
 Vote: Kohan – yes; Leonardo – yes; Seichter – yes; Sanders – yes; Chairman  
 Fitzsimmons  – yes . 
 
PUBLIC HEARINGS 
1. Text Amendment request for Quinnipiac Valley Growth Partners to add cannabis retailer 
as an allowed use by Special Permit in the I-40 (Industrial) Zoning District. Text 
amendment will alter Sections §4.8.C and §6.34.  #507-26 
Commissioner Leonardo read the legal notice.  #507-26 – Text Amendment request for Quinnipiac Valley 
Growth Partners to add cannabis retailer as an allowed use by Special Permit in the I-40 (Industrial) 
Zoning District. The Text Amendment will alter Sections §4.8.C and §6.34. A copy of the text amendment 
can be found in the Planning and Zoning Office. Correspondence included a draft of the amendment;  
letter dated October 21, 2026, from Susan Beckman, Regional Planner, Lower Connecticut River Valley 
Council of Governments, to Wallingford Planning and Zoning; Inspection Report from the Fire Marshal 
dated October 27, 2026; letter received November 4, 2026, from Naugatuck Valley Council of
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 2 
 
Governments, to Wallingford Planning and Zoning; letter dated November 5, 2026, from Cheryl 
DiGenova. 
 
Atty. Dennis Ceneviva, Ceneviva Law Firm, 721 Broad Street, Meriden, presented with Jerry Farrell, Jr., 
and Jim Weaver, partners in Quinnipiac Valley Growth Partners. 
 
Atty. Ceneviva explained that this amendment is designed to permit, in a limited capacity, the retail sale 
of permitted cannabis products. It incorporates comments from the Town Planner and the Commission.  
The proposed amendment requires a Special Permit and gives the Commission substantial breadth in 
approving. It will allow up to three businesses to limit proliferation and limits the use to the I-40 zone.  
The use will not be allowed within 1000 linear ft of a residential zone or school or 500 linear ft. from a 
place of worship. They recognized the Commission's concern with the location in a primary commercial 
zone. This creates a use within the I-40 zone that is substantially less impactful than other allowed uses. 
The Town will receive a 3% municipal tax.  There is nothing different in the concept that was presented 
before except for the location. In the recent elections, Massachusetts had an attempt to reverse the 
legalization of recreational marijuana, but it failed by a wide margin. 
 
Mr. Weaver stated that the 3% tax is in addition to the State sales and excise taxes.  This applies only to 
adult use sales, not the medical use sales. They believe there will be a market in Wallingford.  This will 
redeploy vacant space.  They expect to employ 11 people who will be paid competitively.  These are 
tangible economic benefits.  
 
Mr. Farrell stated that they understand that putting the retailer in a primarily commercial area is not 
appropriate.  The I-40 zone is more appropriate.   
 
Commissioner Seichter noted comments made at the August public hearing indicating that things have 
changed since cannabis was prohibited in 2021.  Public Act 20-21 legalized recreational cannabis in the 
State but gave towns the option to regulate it, deny the approved use, or do nothing, which would mean 
that cannabis is an approved use. The Town had a public hearing, and many spoke in favor of the 
regulation.  It passed unanimously. He stated that his position has not changed. This is another 
opportunity to decide where the Town will go.  A similar application was denied in the Spring because 
our regulations state that any use must be legal under local, state, and Federal laws.  He gets that the 
State can regulate cannabis, but the Federal government has the right to enforce its laws.  He is not 
swayed because other municipalities have approved it or because it will bring the Town revenue.  If this 
is approved, the Commission needs to do away with the regulation banning cannabis because it won’t 
make sense. He is opposed to this application. 
 
Commissioner Sanders stated that he is opposed. This is the third time this has been discussed.   There is 
a distinction between medical use and recreational use.  The Federal government rescheduled medical 
marijuana but did not decriminalize marijuana.  If the request were based on medical marijuana, that 
would be something that can be discussed. Wallingford has a choice. This will have lasting 
consequences.  He noted the 3% tax revenue.  Mr. Weaver agreed that in any business, the big winner is
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 3 
 
the business.  The State designed the program to remunerate communities.  He stated that there are 
currently people in Wallingford using cannabis.  Those products are often unregulated and untested.  
Having a store in town will move people away from the unregulated products.  Commissioner Sanders 
stated that the big winner in this is the State, with 10% excise plus sales tax.  What is the cost to 
Wallingford?  The Town is already negatively impacted by recreational marijuana use.  Substance abuse 
is already a problem.  Regulations are guardrails to protect people.  Once the product leaves your 
premises, the Town is responsible for dealing with irresponsible consumption.  He wants to know what 
the residents want.  
 
Commissioner Benham asked about the regulations on the cannabis retailers from the Department of 
Consumer Protection.  Mr. Farrell stated that a cannabis retailer is almost analogous to a pharmacy.  The 
supply chain is very regulated. They won’t be producers but will rely on licensed producers in 
Connecticut that provide pharmaceutical-grade products.  The consumer should be able to rely on the 
fact that the product they consume is regulated.  The State legislature made the cannabis marketplace 
so consumers can rely on it. This is a highly regulated marketplace, not a smoke shop. Customers have 
to show ID and be on camera, as well as staff.  There is high security.   
 
Commissioner Camire questioned the need for the carve-out retailers. Mr. Farrell replied that there are 
only so many licenses in the State.  He doesn’t see a producer coming to Wallingford.  Commissioner 
Camire clarified that under State law, this is legal. Mr. Farrell confirmed.  Mr. Camire asked if package 
stores can sell THC beverages.  Mr. Farrell replied yes. It is allowed in the license.  Commissioner Camire 
asked how they will handle cash.  Mr. Weaver replied that there are retail platforms that will help 
manage everything from inventory to cash.  He stated that cash has to be tracked like the product. 
There will be surveillance in place.  The volume of transactions will be less than a liquor store. 
Commissioner Camire stated that he had mixed feelings on this issue. There is evidence that cannabis 
use can trigger psychotic episodes in those genetically predisposed.  Under Federal Law, this is still a 
Schedule I drug.  It is worth considering carving out just retailers or just allowing all cannabis 
establishments.  He asked where smoke shops are regulated and if some aspects of this regulation 
would apply to them as well, including the required distance from residential areas and schools. If we 
are going to do this, he would like a more comprehensive look.  Enforcement is tricky. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo stated that he also has mixed feelings.  He likes the location better and the 
Special Permit, which gives the Commission more leeway.  We should reevaluate vape and smoke shops.  
He thinks we need more regulation.  He does not see this changing use, and a denial won’t mean there 
will be no cannabis use in Town.  Does this fit the character of the Town?   
 
Commissioner Kohan clarified that the retailer would be open seven days a week.  He appreciates the 
change to the I-40 zone.  He noted that the debate on cannabis has been going on since the 1800s. The 
Federal Government still hasn’t allowed cannabis research.  The State went through the same argument 
when they passed Bill 12-01 allowing cannabis sales in chapter 4.20.H.  The State decided that it’s okay. 
This is a business decision, not a health decision.  The State does regulate what can be displayed as 
signage on the establishment. It is legal in Connecticut.
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 4 
 
 
Commissioner Camire likes the degree of signage regulation and wants it applied to smoke shops.  
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons quoted the purpose of zoning regulations:  “The function of this board is to 
regulate the height, number of stories and size of buildings and other structures, the percentage of the 
area of the lot that may be occupies, the size of yards, courts and other open spaces, the density of 
population, and the location and use of buildings, structures, and land for trade, industry, residence and 
other purposes, to regulate the height, size and location of advertising signs and billboards within the 
limits of the Town, to divide the town into districts of such number, shape and area as may be best 
suited to carry out the purposes of the statute, to regulate the erection, construction, reconstruction, 
alteration, and use of buildings or structures and the use of land in accordance with a comprehensive 
plan, to lessen congestion in the streets, to secure safety from fire, panic and other dangers, to promote 
health and the general welfare, to provide adequate light and air, to prevent the overcrowding of land, 
to avoid undue concentration of population, to facilitate adequate provision of transportation, water, 
sewerage, schools, parks, and other public requirements with full consideration of the character of the 
districts and their suitability for particular uses, to protect historically , architecturally and culturally 
significant buildings and sites, to encourage energy-efficient patterns of development, encourage use of 
solar and other renewable forms of energy, protect subsurface water supplies and protect against 
sedimentation of waterways and erosion caused by wind, rain and water movement, and to conserve 
the value of buildings, encourage the most appropriate use of land throughout said Town.” He stated 
that this is a land use board.  The Economic Development Commission reported that this is an industry 
providing jobs. This is a text amendment.  In 2021, cannabis was discussed at the request of the Office of 
the Mayor, and the Commission had to make a determination.  Now we can think about changing the 
regulations.  He noted the number of businesses that are licensed to sell liquor and firearms in town.  
Whether you are for or against, they are all licensed.  The revised amendment takes into account the 
Commission’s feedback, and the use will only be allowed by Special Permit.  It will not be close to a 
residence, schools, or churches.   
 
Mr. Pagini stated that in 2021 he was given guidance from the Mayor’s office to prohibit cannabis.  Now 
there is no guidance from the Mayor. The decision is up to the Commission. 
 
PUBLIC COMMENT 
William Butka stated that he was active in law enforcement for 46 years. He is opposed to any change 
that will allow the sale or production of cannabis.  This opens the floodgates.  Cannabis has negative 
impacts on public health.  He read some current headlines regarding recreational marijuana and quoted 
from a study. Training police officers to be certified drug recognition experts is expensive.  Will the 
potential revenue offset the cost of lives? It’s up to us to protect public health. 
 
Natalie Melma spoke on behalf of her daughter, Valerie Melma.  She is opposed to the change. She 
works in substance abuse prevention. Valerie’s father misused marijuana, and there have been 
consequences to the family.  The marijuana being produced is very strong.  Adults already have access in
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 5 
 
nearby communities.  She asked the Commission to consider the cost to families and caregivers. This 
expands the availability. 
 
Cheryl DeGenova stated that she cares deeply about the health and safety of the community.  She is 
concerned with recreational cannabis.  In 2021, this Commission voted to prohibit cannabis 
establishments.  What has changed since then?  What benefit outweighs the risk?  She asked the 
Commission to maintain the prohibition. 
 
Rocco DeGenova, 7 Regent Court, stated that he serves on the Wallingford Committee on Aging. He 
went to the Senior Center and spoke to the seniors.  They don’t support a cannabis dispensary.  They 
have seen the negative effects of recreational cannabis on young lives.   
 
Rep. Mary Mushinsky stated that her main concern is the effect on academic advancement and the 
workforce.  Cannabis use affects critical brain function, learning capacity, and workforce readiness.  
National data show that 80% of new users are between the ages of 12 and 20.  Regular use in young 
people can lead to a drop in IQ, reduced motivation, and reduced earning potential.  This affects 
employers as well.  This is not a good fit for Wallingford.  
 
Shawn Doherty, Executive Director of the Wallingford Family YMCA, noted that the YMCA recognizes 
that cannabis is legal under Connecticut law.  He asked if the proposed amendment is consistent with 
the vision of the POCD. The YMCA provides safe places and promotes healthy lifestyles.  Expanding 
opportunities for cannabis retail does not advance community goals. On behalf of the YMCA Board, 
staff, volunteers, and members, he asked the Commission to uphold the vision of a healthy, family-
friendly Wallingford. 
 
William Dickenson, 112 Grieb Road, stated that he opposes the application.  He noted that the 
Connecticut Health Department is silent on this issue of medical marijuana.  The FDA hasn’t tested 
marijuana.  It is not prescribed by a doctor with specific dosages.  The health risks include addiction, 
abnormal brain development, and cannabis psychosis. We need a lot more information.  He shared a 
recent CDC alert.  
 
Diane Mark with the Coalition for Better Wallingford stated that they opposed the application.  They run 
targeted prevention programs in schools, among other programs. Opening this would actively undo 
their work.  A storefront gives a false sense that it is risk-free.  Cannabis compromises mental health and 
puts a strain on local health services. This will fundamentally alter the Wallingford character of a proud 
family-first community.  Today’s cannabis contains higher levels of THC.  
 
Nicolina Kotto, youth representative to the Coalition for Better Wallingford, stated that the Commission 
needs to consider how this will affect younger generations.  Does normalizing cannabis align with 
encouraging healthy habits?  She understands that there are economic benefits, but that shouldn’t be 
the priority.  If there are dispensaries in town, that implies it’s okay.
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 6 
 
Patricia Cole, 50 North Street, stated that she is opposed. She doesn’t believe that there is a need for 
more dispensaries.  Today’s products are more potent than in the past.  She read from a Yale study 
published earlier this year regarding marijuana and motor vehicle fatalities.  There has been an increase 
in fatalities associated with cannabis use.  Users will find a way to get it.  The Town should not facilitate 
it. 
 
Alexandria Johnson, North Main Street, stated that she opposes the application.  She knows the damage 
done by marijuana use.  Keep the strict regulations as they are.  You read that the purpose includes 
health and wellness as well as where to place these things. 
 
Jessica Wysocki, 76 Knollwood Drive, reminded the Commission that there is no such thing as legalized 
distribution of marijuana.  The Town must follow Federal code or will be legally liable for damages.  She 
likes investing in health and public safety.  
 
Bob Gross, Long Hill Road, stated that he’d be surprised if this was approved. He doesn’t see the benefit 
to the Town. 
 
Ms. Mushinsky read a statement from Rajan Doring, Sherhan Drive. The Commission needs to ask what 
they want Wallingford to be. Cannabis retailers don’t advance the vision.  The town already has 
substance abuse problems. Planning & Zoning decisions shape what Wallingford will look like in the 
future.  Strengthen the town by investing in people.  
 
Atty. Ceneviva thanked the public for their heartfelt comments.  He stated that the State has permitted 
the use of cannabis and that the State of Massachusetts just re-approved its law allowing it. This is an 
opportunity to provide cannabis in a regulated fashion. It will not be sold to children. Cannabis is more 
regulated than alcohol.  
 
Mr. Farrell stated that this is a regulated market, which is better than an unregulated market.  
 
Mr. Weaver agreed that there are problematic uses.  The State has taken that into account. There are 
allotment limits. The dosages are restricted.  The staff will be on the lookout for problematic use.  Their 
low- to moderate concentration products are for responsible adult use. 
 
Hearing no further public comment, Chairman Fitzsimmons called for a motion to close the public 
hearing. 
 
Commissioner Kohan: Motion to close the public hearing for application #507-26 – Section 
§6.34 7 §4.8.C – Cannabis Retailers for a Zoning Text Amendment to Sections §6.34 and 
4.8.C.14. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo:  second 
Vote: Unanimous
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 7 
 
 
Commissioner Sanders stated that once the cannabis leaves the premises, the Town is responsible for 
the outcomes.  He thanked the public that spoke. He suggested adding to the Motion that Section 
4.16.C, item 4, be revised to include preschools, early childhood education centers, and day care 
facilities instead of just schools. He also suggested standardizing all the distances to 1,000 ft. 
 
Commissioner Seichter noted that the public is not in favor of this application. Every Town can make its 
own decision. He doesn’t see the benefit to the community. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo stated that he supports the Federal government looking at the safety of 
cannabis.  We are not changing the demand for cannabis, just allowing the use of something people are 
already using.  At the end of the day, cannabis is already in town.  We aren’t stopping it by denying this 
application. 
 
Commissioner Kohan stated that it sounds like Wallingford has a drug problem with five substance 
abuse organizations.  This retailer would not increase the demand.  One legalized retailer won’t change 
things.  Wallingford used to be known for the most bars and package stores per capita in the State.  He 
supports this as a business decision. This is a highly regulated business.  The applicant will make sure it’s 
well run. 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons thanked the public for coming out and providing input.  He stated that this is a 
land use application.  State law made it possible.  The request is to add a retail use, not a dispensary. 
This is a first step.  Next would be the Special Permit application. This would be allowed only in this 
industrial zone.  This is a permissible product according to the State of Connecticut.  
 
Commissioner Kohan clarified the change to the school definition in Section 4.14.C item 4 and stated 
that he will leave the distances as is. 
 
Mr. Farrell replied that he would accept that. 
 
Commissioner Kohan: Motion to approve application #507-26 – Section §6.34 and §4.8.C – 
Cannabis Retailer for a Zoning Text Amendment to Sections §6.34 and 4.8.C.14 to add 
Cannabis Retailer as an allowed use by Special Permit in the I-40 9industrial District on 
language dated October 7, 2026 with the addition of Section C item E with the addition of 
preschool, daycare and early childhood education centers added, because of the legalization 
of cannabis in Connecticut through Senate Bill 12.01 codified under Chapter 4.20.H regulation 
of adult use cannabis as such that this text amendment will allow for a viable business 
opportunity in Wallingford. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo:  Second 
Vote: Kohan – yes; Leonardo – yes; Seichter – no; Sanders – no; Chairman Fitzsimmons  – yes. 
The application is approved.
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 8 
 
2. Text Amendment request for KSCGH Partners LLC to add a new section §4.27 entitled “Mixed 
Use (MU) District” floating zone to the Town of Wallingford Zoning Regulations   #505-26 
Commissioner Leonardo noted the new correspondence including a draft amendment dated October 28, 
2026; an email dated November 3, 2026 from Rachel Shamaly, Zoning Enforcement Officer, to Kevin 
Pagini, Town Planner; a document of changes and explanations dated November 3, 2026. 
 
Atty. Dennis Ceneviva, Ceneviva Law Firm, 721 Broad Street, Meriden, presented the revised 
amendment. He noted that this is a continuation and that the revised draft was distributed.  The 
revisions are based on comments from the prior meeting.  These include limiting potential locations to 
the WI and IX zones, as well as prohibiting uses including pawn shops, cannabis sales at retail, vape and 
smoke shops, and massage parlors. They removed the term ‘character’ from Section F.2 and replaced it 
with potential impact.  Regarding the minimum size, Town staff felt 40 acres was appropriate, but it 
doesn’t matter to his client.  The concept is to have a nice mixed-use district like the one in Cheshire. 
They want to give the Commission latitude. The applicant will need to bring a conceptual site plan to an 
informal meeting with staff first.  
 
Commissioner Camire asked about the gross floor minimums of 25% residential and 25% commercial.  
Atty. Ceneviva replied that the concern was that nothing would be 90%. This would be an overall master 
plan. Other towns have used minimums to get mixed use.  Commissioner Camire clarified that the 
underlying zones have been changed to just the WI and IX.  Atty. Ceneviva replied that the change was 
based on conversations with the Town Planner. They made certain the underlying requirements will 
remain unless modified by the Commission. The underlying uses wouldn’t be the same, but other 
regulations would stay, such as watershed protection. Commissioner Camire stated concern about 
avoiding spot zoning and asked if there is a list of potential parcels in town.  Mr. Pagini replied that he 
has identified 6 possible properties with at least 40 acres; whether all 40 can be developed or not is 
something else.  Commissioner Camire clarified that the property the applicant owns would work. He 
asked about the change to apartment sizes to avoid restricting it to 1-bedroom and studio.  Atty. 
Ceneviva stated that suggestion came from the Commission. Commissioner Camire asked about the 150 
ft. buffer width and setbacks.  Mr. Pagini replied that it is based on comments from the public.  They 
also wanted a 150 ft distance to residential, and the WI currently has a 60 ft. setback. The intent was to 
buffer the existing residential properties.  Atty. Ceneviva stated that for the buffer along Rt. 68, the 
Town staff wanted to avoid large parking lots at the road to make the property more attractive.  This 
gives the Commission flexibility to consider the impact.  Commissioner Camire asked if the 50% open 
space is standard.  Mr. Pagini replied that it came from the Town Engineer and Water & Sewer. They are 
concerned with overall impervious surface.  Commissioner Camire noted that this proposal fits with the 
POCD.  
 
Commissioner Leonardo stated that 40 acres seems fine, but he is open to increasing it to 60 acres. He 
asked about building height and whether it can be reduced from 50 ft. Atty. Ceneviva noted that it is a 
maximum. As the plan comes together, the Commission can look at where it fits in the surrounding area.  
It was reduced from the maximum in the underlying zone.
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 9 
 
Commissioner Kohan said this floating zone is a major undertaking. He stated that this gives the 
Commission legislative power and broad discretion. He stated that he looked at Guilford’s mixed-use 
regulation and suggested including the following purpose statement: “to permit and facilitate a 
development of comprehensively planned mixed-use development”, and stated that this includes 
certain types of businesses and residential uses. He noted that this proposal uses a maximum density of 
ten units where Guilford used six. Permitted uses in the Guilford regulations include outpatient medical 
facilities, research labs, and vet offices.  They list several accessory uses and structures such as outdoor 
dining and satellite receivers.  He suggested that building design reviews be done before the plan is 
submitted.  He also suggested requiring a statement on how the development relates to the neighboring 
areas and the potential impact.  Under residential requirements, he suggested adding buffering to 
residential district boundary lines and buildings, roadways, driveways, parking areas, and signs.  Overall, 
he thinks the text amendment is good. 
 
Atty. Ceneviva noted that he looked at Guilford’s and other towns’ regulations.  He stated that a lot of 
what was mentioned is already in there, just worded differently.  He didn’t include a comprehensive list 
of permitted uses, including other uses determined by the Commission that are consistent with the 
intent of these regulations. That provides more flexibility. He noted that a narrative statement is already 
part E.2, the zone change application. The statement includes the proposed uses, special design 
considerations, architectural themes, and how it is consistent with the surrounding area. The proposal 
will be comprehensive.  In E.1, there is an informal process to review issues with design before the plan 
is presented formally. The Commission can approve, modify, or deny an application.   
 
Commissioner Seichter noted that some of the items mentioned at the last meeting are not included in 
the changes.  He is concerned that the development could end up being 75% commercial. He would like 
the minimum residential percentage to be increased to 35%.  He would like the setback for Rt. 68 to be 
100 ft. and the setback for residential should be 150 ft.  He stated that he is not in favor of drive-through 
businesses. He stated that he sees some benefits and recognizes the guardrails.  
 
Atty. Ceneviva stated that a minimum of 35% residential is not inappropriate.  He stated that the 
setback for Rt. 68 was a collaborative decision. The number is a minimum. The intent is to make it look 
more like a town setting. Commissioner Seichter noted that it reads “not greater than,” so it is a 
maximum. Atty. Ceneviva noted that any development on Rt. 68 would require an OSTA permit due to 
new curb cuts.  They want to avoid a lot of parking in the front. 
 
Commissioner Sanders asked what problem this solves.  Does it add complexity to the regulations?  
When applied, does it adhere to the underlying zone or provide autonomy to the site from the zone?  
Atty. Ceneviva replied that the bulk standards that are not changed by this amendment would still apply.  
Commissioner Sanders stated concern that it appears to be hard for developers to have an informal 
conversation with the Town.  He asked if the word ‘shall’ should be replaced with ‘may’ in the 
introduction where it says ‘shall a floating zone be applied'. He stated that he would like to see more 
than a 35% residential minimum.  Regarding the section on prohibited uses, how is ‘significant’ being 
defined?  Atty. Ceneviva stated that there was intent to put in language which gives the Commission
November 9, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 10 
 
protection. Significant means more than 50%. Commissioner Sanders suggested including libraries, 
gaming halls, pool halls, and churches as permitted.  He stated concern with subdivision and asked how 
that would work.  Atty. Ceneviva replied that they would have to file a subdivision application. The OCSP 
would be fully effective. One developer could take the residential component, and another take the 
commercial.  The plan wouldn’t change, just the owner. Commissioner Sanders asked if there is any 
detriment to looking at re-subdivision to see if it should be permissible. A different applicant could come 
with an aggregation of properties and then break them up after the approval, then do something in 
conflict with the underlying zone. Atty. Ceneviva stated that that can’t happen, as they have to provide 
an overall Conceptual Site Plan for approval. If modified, they would need to come back with the 
modification.  The concept gives the Commission flexibility. Who does the building is not relevant.  
Commissioner Sanders stated that he wouldn’t want the property split apart afterwards.  Regarding the 
heights of 50 ft., this is more than is allowed in the WI and IX zones.  They allow increases based on 
increased setback. There are reasons the building heights are there.  He would prefer to see the 
underlying zone drive the building heights. He asked if there should be setbacks between buildings 
within the property.  He suggested allowing the underlying zone setbacks to apply to borders. Regarding 
the number of bedrooms, this needs to be clarified to get closer to the spirit requested.  For the front 
yard setback on Rt. 68, in the WI it is 200 ft; in the IX it is 60 ft.  Regarding the statement ‘open space 
unless reduced by the Commission’. Future Commissions end up with something subjective instead of 
being guided by regulation.  This needs to be tightened.  
 
Mr. Pagini noted that the difference between ‘may’ and ’shall’ is defined in the regulations. Shall is 
mandatory. May is permissive.   
 
PUBLIC COMMENT 
Jessica Wysocki, 72 Knollwood Drive, stated that floating zones violate planning and zoning regulatory 
code if applied discriminately. Standards must be publicly published for each zone. The Commission
